headline.text:
YOU'RE SITTING IN A MEETING.

THE ROOM IS FINE.

THEN SUDDENLY —
YOU'RE ON FIRE.
ESTROGEN IS FALLING.

body.text: Lower estradiol can disrupt the brain's temperature-control centre, making small temperature changes trigger a hot flash.

WHAT CAN HELP:
Cooling, layered clothing, sleep support — and for bothersome symptoms, clinician-guided menopause treatment.

YOU WAKE UP SOAKED.

CHANGE YOUR CLOTHES.
CHANGE THE SHEETS.

THEN TRY TO SLEEP AGAIN.
ESTROGEN + TEMPERATURE CONTROL.

body.text: Falling estradiol can trigger night sweats and repeated awakenings.

WHAT CAN HELP:
Keep the room cool, identify triggers, protect sleep — and discuss treatment if symptoms are persistent.

headline.text:
EARLY.
LATE.
HEAVY.
LIGHT.

YOUR PERIOD HAS COMPLETELY LOST THE PLOT.
PROGESTERONE IS BECOMING LESS PREDICTABLE.

body.text: Ovulation becomes irregular during perimenopause, so progesterone production can fluctuate.
Estradiol can also swing dramatically.

WHAT CAN HELP:
Track bleeding. Heavy or unusual bleeding deserves clinical assessment.

HERE'S WHY EVERYONE IS ANNOYING YOU LATELY.

YES.

EVEN THE PERSON BREATHING TOO LOUD.
ESTROGEN + YOUR BRAIN.

body.text: Estradiol interacts with brain systems involved in mood regulation.
Fluctuating estrogen plus poor sleep can make irritability feel much stronger.

WHAT CAN HELP:
Prioritise sleep, movement and stress support — and seek clinical help if mood symptoms are persistent or severe.

ESTROGEN + COGNITION.

body.text: Estradiol affects brain networks involved in memory and attention.
Hormonal fluctuation, especially with poor sleep, can contribute to brain fog.

WHAT CAN HELP:
Protect sleep, exercise regularly and review medications, mood and other causes with your clinician.

YOU GET INTO BED.

“NOPE.”
ESTROGEN + PROGESTERONE + SLEEP.

body.text: Hormonal changes can affect sleep directly — and hot flashes can keep waking you.

WHAT CAN HELP:
Consistent sleep timing, exercise and a cool room help.
Persistent insomnia deserves proper assessment and treatment.

YOU'VE NEVER BEEN THIS ANXIOUS.

YOUR MIND WON'T SWITCH OFF.

AND YOU CAN'T EXPLAIN WHY.
ESTROGEN + THE BRAIN.

body.text: Changing estradiol can influence neurotransmitter systems involved in mood and anxiety.
Sleep disruption can amplify it.

WHAT CAN HELP:
CBT, exercise and clinician-guided treatment can help — especially when symptoms are persistent.

YOU'RE NOT RUNNING.

YOU'RE NOT EXERCISING.

BUT YOUR HEART IS POUNDING.
ESTROGEN + AUTONOMIC REGULATION.

body.text: Palpitations can occur alongside menopausal hot flashes and anxiety.

WHAT CAN HELP:
Track when they happen and what triggers them.
NEW, severe or persistent palpitations need medical assessment — don't assume hormones are the cause.

YOUR KNEES HURT.

YOUR HIPS HURT.

YOUR HANDS HURT.

“AM I JUST GETTING OLD?”
ESTROGEN + MUSCULOSKELETAL HEALTH.

body.text: Estrogen receptors are found in bone, muscle and connective tissue.
Its decline may contribute to musculoskeletal symptoms.

WHAT CAN HELP:
Strength training, adequate protein, healthy weight management and assessment of persistent pain.

YOUR BONES DON'T HURT WHEN THEY'RE LOSING DENSITY.

THAT'S THE SCARY PART.
ESTROGEN PROTECTS BONE REMODELLING.

body.text: After menopause, lower estradiol increases bone turnover and can accelerate bone loss.

WHAT CAN HELP:
Resistance training, adequate calcium/vitamin D intake and bone-density assessment when indicated.

YOU'RE EATING THE SAME.

MOVING THE SAME.

BUT YOUR WAISTLINE HAS OTHER PLANS.
ESTROGEN + METABOLISM.

body.text: Lower estrogen is associated with a shift toward more abdominal fat during midlife.
But ageing, muscle, sleep, diet and activity matter too.

WHAT CAN HELP:
Strength training, protein-rich meals, movement and sleep — not crash dieting.

YOU STILL LOVE YOUR PARTNER.

YOU'RE STILL ATTRACTED TO THEM.

BUT YOUR LIBIDO?

GONE.
ESTROGEN + TESTOSTERONE + CONTEXT.

body.text:
Lower estrogen can cause dryness and pain.
Androgens contribute to sexual desire for some women.
Sleep, stress, mood and medications matter too.

WHAT CAN HELP:
Treat pain/dryness first and discuss persistent low desire clinically.

YOU WANT TO HAVE SEX.

BUT IT HURTS.

SO YOU STOP WANTING TO HAVE SEX.
ESTROGEN IS A BIG PART OF THIS.

body.text: Lower estrogen can make vaginal tissue thinner, drier and less elastic.

WHAT CAN HELP:
Lubricants and moisturisers can help.
Persistent symptoms may benefit from clinician-guided local vaginal estrogen or other treatments.

headline.text:
YOU KNOW EVERY TOILET BETWEEN HOME AND WORK.

BECAUSE YOU HAVE TO.
ESTROGEN + THE URINARY TRACT.

body.text: Lower estrogen can affect vaginal, urethral and bladder tissues.

WHAT CAN HELP:
Pelvic-floor assessment, bladder strategies and — when appropriate — local vaginal estrogen can help genitourinary symptoms.

YOUR HOT FLASHES GOT BETTER.

BUT THE DRYNESS DIDN'T.

IN FACT, IT GOT WORSE.
LOW ESTROGEN CAN PERSIST AFTER MENOPAUSE.

body.text: Genitourinary symptoms can continue or worsen because the tissues remain in a low-estrogen environment.

WHAT CAN HELP:
Moisturisers, lubricants and clinician-guided local treatment can make a real difference.

headline.text:
MENOPAUSE ISN'T ONLY AN ESTROGEN STORY.

WHAT HAPPENS TO TESTOSTERONE?
TESTOSTERONE DECLINES GRADUALLY.

body.text: It does not suddenly disappear at menopause.
Androgens contribute to sexual function, muscle and other physiological processes.

WHAT CAN HELP:
Strength training, adequate protein and addressing sleep, mood and medication factors.

“MY ESTROGEN IS LOW.”

OK.

BUT WHAT ABOUT PROGESTERONE?

AND TESTOSTERONE?
MENOPAUSE CHANGES THE WHOLE HORMONAL PICTURE.

body.text:
ESTROGEN ↓
PROGESTERONE ↓
TESTOSTERONE ↓ GRADUALLY
The timing and pattern are different for each hormone.
THAT'S WHY SYMPTOMS DON'T ARRIVE IN ONE NEAT PACKAGE.

YOUR PERIODS ARE CHAOTIC.

AND YOU KEEP HEARING:
“IT'S ALL ESTROGEN.”
PROGESTERONE CHANGES WITH OVULATION.

body.text: During perimenopause, ovulation becomes less predictable.
Less ovulation = less consistent progesterone production.

WHAT CAN HELP:
Track cycles and symptoms. Persistent sleep or bleeding problems deserve clinical assessment.

BRAIN FOG.

TERRIBLE SLEEP.

WHAT CHANGED?
ESTROGEN DOESN'T JUST “DROP.”

body.text: During perimenopause, estradiol can swing dramatically before settling at lower postmenopausal levels.

WHAT CAN HELP:
Track symptoms over time rather than judging yourself by one bad day.

body.text:
Hot flashes can wake you.
Poor sleep raises stress.
Stress can make sleep harder.

WHAT CAN HELP:
Treat the sleep problem at its source — behavioural support, CBT-I and appropriate menopause treatment can all be considered.

YOU'RE EXHAUSTED.

SO SOMEONE TELLS YOU:

“YOUR CORTISOL IS THE PROBLEM.”
NOT SO FAST.

body.text: Cortisol is your body's major stress hormone — but menopause does not simply mean “high cortisol.”
Sleep disruption, hot flashes and life stress can interact with the stress system.

WHAT CAN HELP:
Sleep, exercise, stress-management and clinical assessment when fatigue persists.

body.text: But fatigue can also come from anaemia, thyroid disease, sleep disorders, medications, depression and other conditions.

WHAT CAN HELP:
If fatigue is persistent, ask for a proper clinical assessment rather than guessing which hormone is responsible.

ESTROGEN + PROGESTERONE CAN DRIVE IRREGULAR BLEEDING.

body.text: But heavy, prolonged or unusual bleeding can have other causes.

Track the pattern and get assessed when bleeding is heavy, persistent, new or concerning.

BUT YOUR HORMONES DIDN'T JUST DISAPPEAR.
ESTROGEN + PROGESTERONE + ANDROGENS CHANGE.

body.text: After menopause, estradiol and progesterone remain low.
Androgens continue to circulate and gradually decline with age.

WHAT CAN HELP:
Think long-term: bones, muscle, cardiovascular health, sexual health and persistent symptoms.

DRY?
ACHY?
NOT SLEEPING?
LOW ESTROGEN CAN HAVE LONG-TERM EFFECTS.

body.text:
Some symptoms fade.
Others persist.
Genitourinary symptoms are particularly likely to continue without treatment.

WHAT CAN HELP:
Don't wait it out — discuss persistent symptoms and evidence-based options with a clinician.

body.text: Cardiovascular risk is influenced by many factors, including blood pressure, lipids, glucose, body composition and ageing.

WHAT CAN HELP:
Know your numbers. Exercise. Don't smoke. Manage BP, cholesterol and glucose.

Menopause-related brain fog is common.

Sleep, exercise, cardiovascular risk management and assessment of persistent cognitive changes.
